session_1758602281416_yvmapma: To what extent do you support or oppose universal healthcare policies that provide government-funded healthcare coverage for all citizens? Please explain your reasoning.
column3: I strongly support universal health care because it means everyone's covered, period, instead of millions of people cycling in and out of insurance and having the uninsured rate tick up again. It would cut medical debt for people, which is a huge amount of Americans, and it will keep people from putting off needed health care because they can't afford it.

session_1758602281416_yvmapma: What do you think are the most significant impacts, positive or negative, of implementing a universal healthcare system?
column3: The biggest positives are that everyone gets covered and people don't go broke over medical bills and care is more consistent. The negatives, I guess, could be higher taxes, possibly wait times for some services like in other countries. But overall, I think the tradeoff is better health and security for everyone in this country.

session_1758602281416_yvmapma: How do you think universal healthcare policies might affect healthcare quality and accessibility?
column3: I think universal health care would make care way more acceptable since cost wouldn't keep people from going to the doctor. Quality could actually improve too because more people would get preventive care because they wouldn't have to pay for it instead of waiting until things got serious enough to go to the emergency room. I think the main challenge might be, like I know in other countries there you have to wait for appointment sometime, but overall access and fairness would increase and I think that's more important.

session_1758602281416_yvmapma: What impact do you believe a universal healthcare system might have on medical innovation and research?
column3: A universal healthcare system might slow down some profit-driven discoveries since drug companies and hospitals won't be raking in the same huge amounts of money, but it could also push research in a healthier direction with more focus on treatments people actually need instead of what makes the most money on the latest drug. Overall, it might look different, but it won't disappear.

session_1758602281416_yvmapma: How do you think universal healthcare might affect the economic burden on individuals and families?
column3: It would take a huge weight off of people's shoulders. Families wouldn't have to worry about surprise medical bills or going into debt just to pay for medical needs. And monthly costs like insurance premiums and co-pays would pretty much go away. So even if taxes went up a little bit, it would hopefully be balanced out and people would still save money overall.

session_1758602281416_yvmapma: What role do you believe government should play in healthcare delivery and financing?
column3: I think the government should just do the financing side, just make sure everybody has coverage and that the costs are controlled. But the doctors and hospitals should focus on everything else, on the actual decisions about what care people receive. And that way, the system will be run by health experts instead of by insurance experts.

session_1758602281416_yvmapma: How might healthcare provider concerns factor into decisions about universal healthcare implementation?
column3: Doctors and hospitals might worry about getting paid less or dealing with more rules because the government is more involved. So that might make them not crazy about universal healthcare, but a lot of them might also like not having to fight with insurance companies, and they may prefer knowing that their patients are all being treated the same way and receiving the same care.

session_1758602281416_yvmapma: What economic effects, both positive and negative, might result from transitioning to a universal healthcare system?
column3: On the positive side, people would save money on premiums and co-pays and medical debt. Small businesses wouldn't have to pay for employees to have insurance. I'm sure that's crazy expensive. But on the negative side, taxes would definitely have to go up to pay for it. I guess insurance companies would go out of a job.

session_1758602281416_yvmapma: How do you think the interests of taxpayers versus healthcare consumers should be balanced when making healthcare policy?
column3: I think that balance has to come from remembering that as a taxpayer you are also a health care consumer, so you're paying into something that you're using. It's like paying into social security, you know you're going to use it. So if we eliminate private insurance and everybody's on the same insurance, then it's going to be fair just because we all have the same thing.

session_1758602281416_yvmapma: What role do you think social equity and access to care play in discussions about healthcare policy?
column3: I think social equity and access to care plays a huge role in healthcare policy discussions because it's not just about cost, it's about fairness. Social equity and access to care refers to deciding whether everyone, no matter what their income or background, that they all get the actual treatment that they need. And without focusing on that, the system just keeps widening the gap between who can afford to be healthy and who can't. It really needs to be stopped.

session_1758602281416_yvmapma: How would you describe the relationship between Access to healthcare for all citizens and Support for universal healthcare? Is it a strong or weak connection? Does it have a positive effect (increasing it) or a negative effect (decreasing it)? How strong is this effect?

session_1758602281416_yvmapma: What do you think are the main causes of Support for universal healthcare, and how certain are you about these relationships? Please also indicate if these influences are positive (increasing) or negative (decreasing).
column3: Access to healthcare for all citizens has a strong positive connection with support for universal healthcare. The idea that everyone can see a doctor when they need to is one of the biggest reasons people back it, so it tends to increase support a lot. People mostly support universal healthcare because medical costs are so high and too many people can’t get the care they need. Fairness plays a role too—lots of folks feel healthcare should be a right. On the other hand some worry about higher taxes or not trusting the government to run it well. Overall though, the cost and access issues are the biggest reasons support is strong.

session_1758602281416_yvmapma: Would small changes in Financial protection from medical bills lead to noticeable changes in Support for universal healthcare, or would it take larger shifts? Does it have a positive effect (increasing it) or a negative effect (decreasing it)? How strong is this effect?
column3: I think even small changes in financial protection like fewer surprise bills or less medical debt could noticeably boost support for universal healthcare. The effect would be positive and pretty strong since money stress is one of the biggest reasons people want relief from the government.

session_1758602281416_yvmapma: Is the effect of Better health and security for everyone on Support for universal healthcare immediate, or does it take time to develop? Does it have a positive effect (increasing it) or a negative effect (decreasing it)? How strong is this effect?
column3: I'd say the effect takes a little time, you have to see the health and security benefits play out before people really feel it, but it's definitely positive and pretty strong since once people notice everyone's healthier and more secure support goes way up.

session_1758602281416_yvmapma: Would small changes in Healthcare accessibility lead to noticeable changes in Support for universal healthcare, or would it take larger shifts? Does it have a positive effect (increasing it) or a negative effect (decreasing it)? How strong is this effect?
column3: I don't think small changes in healthcare accessibility will move support much, but I think it would take bigger shifts for people to notice. The effect would be positive when people start to see it, and it will be a strong effect once people start seeing it, but it's gonna have to be a bigger change for people to notice.

session_1758602281416_yvmapma: How would you describe the relationship between Cost as a barrier to care and Support for universal healthcare? Is it a strong or weak connection? Does it have a positive effect (increasing it) or a negative effect (decreasing it)? How strong is this effect?
column3: Cost as a barrier to care has a strong positive connection with support for universal health care. I think the more people feel blocked from quality health care because of their money, the more support goes up. It's one of the biggest drivers behind why people push for it is to get equitable access to quality health care.

session_1758602281416_yvmapma: Is the effect of Medical innovation and research on Support for universal healthcare immediate, or does it take time to develop? Does it have a positive effect (increasing it) or a negative effect (decreasing it)? How strong is this effect?
column3: I'd say the effect takes time because people are going to want to see if universal healthcare will still support innovation and new treatments. It'll be positive if research keeps moving or negative if people think it's slowing down.

session_1758602281416_yvmapma: How confident are you that changes in Economic burden on individuals and families lead to changes in Support for universal healthcare? Does it have a positive effect (increasing it) or a negative effect (decreasing it)? How strong is this effect?
column3: I am very confident that changes in the economic burden on families impact support for universal health care. The effect is going to be positive because the more people are burdened, the more support's going to go up and it's going to be a strong effect since money stress is one of the biggest reasons people want universal coverage in the first place.

session_1758602281416_yvmapma: How would you describe the relationship between Payment reduction and Support for universal healthcare? Is it a strong or weak connection? Does it have a positive effect (increasing it) or a negative effect (decreasing it)? How strong is this effect?
column3: Payment reduction has a positive relationship with support for universal health care. When people see their out-of-pocket costs go down, support goes up. The connection is strong since saving money is one of the biggest reasons people back this idea.

session_1758602281416_yvmapma: How confident are you that changes in Medical debt reduction lead to changes in Support for universal healthcare? Does it have a positive effect (increasing it) or a negative effect (decreasing it)? How strong is this effect?
column3: I am very confident that reducing medical debt increases support for universal health care. It has a positive effect, and the impact is strong, since medical debt is one of the most obvious points of contention driving people toward wanting universal health coverage.

session_1758602281416_yvmapma: How confident are you that changes in Higher taxes lead to changes in Support for universal healthcare? Does it have a positive effect (increasing it) or a negative effect (decreasing it)? How strong is this effect?
column3: I'm pretty confident that higher taxes have a negative effect on support for universal health care. The impact will be moderate to strong depending on how high the taxes are. People are going to worry about how much they'll personally have to pay and they won't know how much they're actually saving on medical bills until they see it happen.

session_1758602281416_yvmapma: How confident are you that changes in Savings on premiums and co-pays lead to changes in Support for universal healthcare? Does it have a positive effect (increasing it) or a negative effect (decreasing it)? How strong is this effect?
column3: I'm very confident that savings on premiums and co-pays have a positive effect on support for universal health care. The effect is strong because cutting everyday costs is one of the biggest reasons people get behind universal health care.

session_1758602281416_yvmapma: Would small changes in Social security analogy lead to noticeable changes in Support for universal healthcare, or would it take larger shifts? Does it have a positive effect (increasing it) or a negative effect (decreasing it)? How strong is this effect?
column3: I think you would need bigger shifts for the social security analogy to really help. It's not something small, it's not something you can really do small. The effect would only be positive if you showed how it's a universal right and you're comparing social security to universal health care. It would be positive if eventually universal health care was thought of the same as social security benefits, but that's like a systemic change kind of thing, not an instant advertising on TikTok kind of thing.

session_1758602281416_yvmapma: Does Access to care have a positive or negative effect on Support for universal healthcare, and how significant is this effect? Does it have a positive effect (increasing it) or a negative effect (decreasing it)? How strong is this effect?
column3: Access to care has a positive effect on support for universal healthcare. When people see more people able to get treatment, support goes up. The effect is strong.

session_1758602281416_yvmapma: Does Healthcare policy have a positive or negative effect on Support for universal healthcare, and how significant is this effect? Does it have a positive effect (increasing it) or a negative effect (decreasing it)? How strong is this effect?
column3: Health care policy has a positive effect on support when it's designed the right way. It has to work with the policy has to work to lower costs. The effect would be strong if the policy was written well. If it's fair and affordable and accessible, then it would be good.

session_1758602281416_yvmapma: Does Systemic gaps have a positive or negative effect on Support for universal healthcare, and how significant is this effect? Does it have a positive effect (increasing it) or a negative effect (decreasing it)? How strong is this effect?
column3: Systemic gaps have a negative effect on support because when people see holes in the system, like people slipping through the cracks, it makes them doubt if the whole thing is really working. And people will just assume the government is inept and they won't support it anymore. The effect would be pretty strong. Because if it's not protecting the people it's supposed to be protecting, then it doesn't deserve to be supported.

session_1758602281416_yvmapma: What factors do you think influence Universal healthcare, and how strong is their impact? Please also indicate if these influences are positive (increasing) or negative (decreasing).
column3: The two biggest things are cost and access. When bills are high or people can't get care, then support for universal health care is going to go way up. And it needs to be fair too since folks are generally on board with the idea of everyone being treated fairly and covered. Also on the other side, higher taxes and not trusting the government will definitely not help support this cause.
